day.head: Before you go
day.say: Pack the night before. A board and a clock if you have them, a pen, and a snack. Nothing else matters.

day.head: The pairing sheet
day.say: A list goes up on the wall each round. Find your name. Beside it is your board number and whether you are White or Black.

day.head: Find your board
day.say: Boards are numbered. Sit on your colour. If somebody is already in your seat, check the sheet again before you say anything.

day.head: Say hello
day.say: Shake hands and say your name. You are about to spend an hour with this person.

day.head: Start the clock
day.say: White moves first, then presses the clock. If White is not there yet, Black starts White’s clock and waits.

day.head: Write it down
day.say: If each player has 30 minutes or more, you must write your moves. Write the move, then play it, or play it and then write. Either is fine.

day.head: If you need help
day.say: Stop both clocks and put your hand up. Wait. Do not shout across the room. The person who comes is the Tournament Director, the TD.

day.head: When it ends
day.say: Shake hands whoever won. Then BOTH of you go and report the result. Do not let the other player report it alone.

day.head: Then you wait
day.say: Rounds start when everybody is finished. Go outside, eat something, and do not talk about your game near the boards.

kit.why: For writing your moves. Bring two.
Rounds are long and there is often no shop.
Only if the tournament asks you to bring them. Most supply them.
A digital one with delay if you have it. Not everybody does.
If you have one. If not, they will sign you up on the day.

sets.name: Touching pieces
sets.blurb: The rule that causes more arguments than every other one put together.

drills.ask: You pick up your knight. Then you see the move loses your queen. What now?

choices.text: You must move that knight, if it has any legal move
Put it back and think again
Ask your opponent if it is all right

drills.why: Touch a piece on purpose and you have to move it. Decide before you reach out.

drills.ask: A piece is sitting crooked, half off its square. You want to straighten it.

choices.text: Say "I adjust" FIRST, then straighten it
Just straighten it, everyone can see what you meant
Straighten it, then say "I adjust"

drills.why: You have to say it before you touch, and it must be your turn. Afterwards is too late.

drills.ask: You touch your bishop. It turns out the bishop has no legal move at all.

choices.text: You may play any legal move you like
You lose your turn
You must move the piece next to it

drills.why: If the piece you touched cannot move, nothing is lost. Play whatever you want.

drills.ask: Your pawn reaches the end. You pick a queen up out of the box, then change your mind and want a knight.

choices.text: Fine. A piece off the board does not count until it lands
Too late, it has to be a queen
You must call the TD

drills.why: There is no penalty for touching a piece that is off the board.

drills.ask: You let go of your rook on a square you did not mean. The move is legal.

choices.text: It stays there. The move is done
You may pick it up again, you did not mean it
It only counts once you press the clock

drills.why: Let go on a legal square and that is your move, even by accident.

drills.ask: Your opponent touches their knight, then moves a pawn instead. You want to say something.

choices.text: Say it now, before you touch anything of your own
Make your move, then mention it
It is too late once they let go

drills.why: A touch-move claim has to come before you touch a piece yourself.

sets.name: The clock
sets.blurb: Two buttons, and about six rules that decide games.

drills.ask: Your opponent’s time runs out. Their flag is down. What happens?

choices.text: Nothing, until you stop the clock and say so
You win automatically, the clock knows
The TD will notice and stop the game

drills.why: Only the two players may call a flag. A TD will never do it for you, and neither may anybody watching.

drills.ask: You want to claim a win on time. How, exactly?

choices.text: Stop both clocks, then say the claim out loud
Point at the flag and keep playing
Put your hand up and shout for the TD

drills.why: Stop both clocks and state it. If they disagree, then put your hand up.

drills.ask: You need the TD. When should you stop the clock?

choices.text: On your own time, not your opponent’s
On theirs, so it costs you nothing
Never stop the clock, just raise your hand

drills.why: You may always stop both clocks to make a claim, and it should be your own time you spend doing it.

drills.ask: You checkmate them. Do you have to press the clock?

choices.text: No. Checkmate ends the game at once
Yes, or the move does not count
You must stop the clock instead

drills.why: Checkmate ends it there and then. Even your own flag falling afterwards does not matter.

drills.ask: Your own flag falls. You have a queen and they have a lone king.

choices.text: You lose. Your flag fell
It is a draw, you were winning
You win, you have more pieces

drills.why: A fallen flag is a fallen flag. Watch the clock as carefully as you watch the board.

drills.ask: They run out of time. All you have left is your king.

choices.text: A draw. You cannot checkmate with a lone king
You win on time
The game carries on

drills.why: You can only win on time if you could ever checkmate. A lone king never can.

sets.name: When it goes wrong
sets.blurb: Pieces fall over. Somebody plays something impossible. Nobody is in trouble.

drills.ask: Four moves ago your opponent moved a knight like a bishop. You have just noticed.

choices.text: Put the position back to before that move and carry on
Too late, it stands
They lose the game

drills.why: Inside the last ten moves, the position goes back. Nobody is punished for a mistake.

drills.ask: The illegal move happened about twenty moves ago.

choices.text: It stands. Play on from here
Go back to it anyway
Start the game again

drills.why: Past ten moves it is too late to unpick. The game carries on.

drills.ask: Your sleeve knocks six pieces over. Whose time do you use to put them back?

choices.text: Yours. Your clock keeps running
Theirs, they can wait
Stop the clock, it was an accident

drills.why: You knocked them over, so you put them back on your own time. Be careful over the board.

drills.ask: You are watching a friend’s game and you spot an illegal move.

choices.text: Say nothing. Only tell the TD, quietly
Tell them, they are your friend
Point at the board so they look

drills.why: People watching must never point things out to the players. That includes parents.

drills.ask: You put your opponent in check. Do you have to say "check"?

choices.text: No. It is up to them to notice
Yes, always
Only in a children’s tournament

drills.why: Saying check is not required and is rare at big events. You may say it, but nobody has to.

sets.name: Draws and endings
sets.blurb: Half a point is a real result. Here is how to claim one.

drills.ask: You want to offer a draw. When?

choices.text: After you move, before you press the clock
Before you move
Any time you like

drills.why: Move, offer, then press. Offering while their clock runs can be called annoying them.

drills.ask: They say no. Ten moves later you would still like a draw.

choices.text: Wait until they offer, or until the position really changes
Ask again, it costs nothing
You may never ask again

drills.why: Asking over and over can be penalised as annoying your opponent.

drills.ask: The same position has now appeared three times. What do you do?

choices.text: Stop both clocks on your turn and claim the draw
The game is drawn by itself
Ask the TD to watch for it

drills.why: It is not automatic. Only the player about to move may claim, and you must say so.

drills.ask: You claim a draw. The TD looks and says you are wrong.

choices.text: Your opponent gets two extra minutes and you play on
You lose the game
Nothing happens

drills.why: A wrong claim costs two minutes, so be sure before you stop the clock.

drills.ask: Only two kings are left on the board.

choices.text: Drawn. Neither side can ever checkmate
Keep playing until the clock runs out
Whoever has more time wins

drills.why: King against king can never be mate, so the game is over as a draw.

drills.ask: Fifty moves each with no capture and no pawn moved. What now?

choices.text: You may claim a draw on your turn
It is drawn automatically at fifty
There is no such rule

drills.why: Fifty moves by EACH side with no capture and no pawn move. You have to claim it.

sets.name: Being a good opponent
sets.blurb: The part people remember about you long after the result.

drills.ask: You have lost. Badly. What do you do first?

choices.text: Shake hands and say well played
Get up and leave
Explain where you went wrong

drills.why: Shake hands whoever won. It is the part of the day everybody remembers.

drills.ask: The game is over. Who reports the result?

choices.text: Both of you go together
The winner
The loser

drills.why: Go together, so there is no argument about what was written down.

drills.ask: Your phone is in your pocket and it rings during the game.

choices.text: Never bring it on. Turn it right off before the round
Silent is fine
It does not matter

drills.why: A phone that makes any noise can cost you the game. Turn it off and leave it in the bag.

drills.ask: You arrive and your game started forty minutes ago.

choices.text: Sit down and play. Your clock has been running
You have lost already
They restart the clock for you

drills.why: You lose only after an hour, or when your time runs out, whichever comes first. Play on.

drills.ask: You are winning easily and your opponent is upset.

choices.text: Play on quietly and finish properly
Tell them what they did wrong
Let them win one back

drills.why: Play the game out without commentary. Talk about it afterwards, if they want to.
